rows.etymology: 90. Kal. aróik ‘to ripen or get fully formed’ as in émi kạạk aróun pái šían ‘this grain has become hard’ < OIA ārohati ‘rises up’. Regarding semantics cf. Kho. ruik ‘to grow (of crops, nails, &c.)’ < OIA ruháti ‘mounts, grows’ (10796).

rows.gloss: this tree has become hollow it seems
rows.etymology: 59. Kal. gúṅgur ‘hollow’ as in šía muṭ gúṅgur húḷa ‘this tree has become hollow it seems’ cf. PIE *gʰegʰ- ‘to curve, bend’. Only IEW: 424 which quotes reflexes in Armenian, Germanic, Baltic, and Iverson and Salmons (1992. 298). Very doubtful.

rows.etymology: 86. Kal. traṅ ‘narrow; tight-fitting (of clothes)’ as in ía phon traṅ ‘this is a narrow path’ < PIE *trenk-¹ ‘to push; to oppress’ (*tronkus ‘thronged’ [IEW]); note e.g. Av. ðrax- tana̢m ‘jammed together’, Middle High German drange, gedrange ‘narrow’, Old Nordic θro̜-n-g-r ‘narrow’ (Köbler). Notes: (a) Here not cognate is somewhat similar-looking Kal. ḍíziḷa vat ‘the place where there are likenesses of goats on the stones’ (with vat < OIA *varta- ‘round stone’ [11348]) and ḍíziḷa (with -(i)ḷa listed in Trail and Cooper as a “3rd person sin- gular and plural past” apparently reflecting OIA -itá-). The first word is used optionally also in the compound ḍíziḷa ḍizáv ‘creator god’. Thus, also ḍizáv means ‘creator god’. The forms with initial retroflex are only found with Trail and Cooper, whereas Morgenstierne has Kal. diz- ‘to create’ which he regards as a borrowing from Kati. Note also Pr. diz ‘Kafir statue of a god’, diz- ‘to create, make’ and past participle dizˈog ‘created; creature’ and dīzga etc. ‘creator’. Au- gusto Cacopardo’s translation of ḍíziḷa vat as ‘the stone of creation’ (2016: 64) goes back to Jettmar’s translation ‘Stein der Erschaffung’ (1975: 382), but the more correct translation is ‘stone of creatures’. (b) Also a different background has somewhat similar-looking Kal. dívaṣa, díbaṣa ‘male goat (one to one and half years old)’ which is a compound that corresponds with Bashg. (Kt.) davašˈa ‘2 year old (24-36 months) male goat’. Strand derives the Kati form with doubts < *dvi-vats-i-ka- ‘two years old’ by which he indi- rectly suggest the unlikely fact that Kati has preserved the original meaning of OIA vatsá-. More plausible is for Kalasha derivation < OIA dvi-varṣa- ‘2 years old’ and for Kati derivation < OIA *dvi-varṣya- (cf. Tor. bašā ‘summer’ < OIA varṣyà- ‘belonging to the Rains’ [11402]). The latter derivation applies also to Pal. divišˈi ‘newly mature male goat (2 years)’.
